Title: Gate the Action, Not the Alert: Checking an Agent Before It Runs
Abstract: Most of the safety tooling around agents is built to tell you what happened. The alert fires, the log line lands, someone reads it, and by then the action has already run. That ordering works when a human is taking the action, because humans hesitate. Agents do not.  I have been shipping AI-generated code to production since I was fourteen, and the thing that changed my practice most was realising that nearly every check I had was on the wrong side of the action. I learned that expensively, in an incident where my alerting worked exactly as designed and was still useless, because it told me about something that had already broken.  This talk is about moving the check earlier. What it actually means to evaluate an action before it executes rather than after. Where you can put that check in a pipeline you already have, rather than in a redesigned one. What it does to your latency and your shipping speed, honestly. And which classes of action are worth gating at all, versus the ones that are cheaper to let fail and revert. I will be specific about the ones I gate and the ones I deliberately do not, because gating everything is its own failure mode.  Tool-agnostic, nothing to install, no product content. For anyone whose agents already have write access to something they care about.

Title: Nobody has written the authorization requirement for MCP agents, so I did
Abstract: I needed to write down what has to be true before an agent's call reaches a production system. I went looking for the requirement to copy, and there isn't one. Everything written on attributing an action to a person assumes a human at a terminal, clicking and watching the system act on their behalf inside one session. Between an agent's instruction and the call that lands downstream there are an arbitrary number of steps that nobody's requirement covers, and the industry still doesn't know how an agent should be identified rather than answering it  So I wrote one, and most of the work went into what the tooling won't do yet. Keycloak's token exchange can widen scope unless you turn a policy on. It records may_act, meaning delegation was permitted, rather than act, meaning it happened. RFC 8707, which MCP has required since June 2025, isn't implemented, so audience binding is configured by hand for each client and its absence produces no error  I'll go through how I ended up classifying integrations by what the downstream system accepts at its authentication interface, not by how critical the operation feels. Then I'll cover the four properties that have to stay separate, because no single mechanism restores all four, and the cases where the honest answer is a written compensating measure instead of a control. If you are writing this down for your own systems, you'll get an argued starting point instead of a blank page.

Title: Hardening AI Coding Agents with Hooks: Enforcing Least Privilege on Autonomous Developers
Abstract: AI coding agents run shell commands, write files, install packages, and spawn subagents: autonomous developers with broad system access. Enforcing least privilege on an agent that needs wide access to be useful is a runtime problem, and it is squarely a DevSecOps one. Sandboxes get disabled because they break real workflows, and system-prompt rules are advisory for a model that wants to finish its task.  This talk presents event-driven hooks as the enforcement layer. Hooks intercept every tool call between the agent's decision and its execution, then allow, deny, or modify it. The hook runs outside the model as a separate process, so prompt injection cannot bypass it. I walk through real blocking scripts (dangerous commands, secret exfiltration, typosquatted installs, agents skip-marking failing tests to fake a green build), map the controls to 6 of the OWASP LLM Top 10, and share benchmarks on keeping synchronous checks under 100ms.  Drawn from an MIT open-source toolkit (481 stars, 1,584 tests) running in production. Demos use Claude Code; the pattern ports to Codex, Copilot, and Cursor.

Title: Blocking What Your Agent Does, Not Just What It Says
Abstract: LLM agents are only as safe as the tools they can reach. Model-side guardrails don't stop an agent from calling execute_sql, exfiltrating a secret through send_email, or crossing a tenant boundary — because the risk lives at the tool call, not the prompt. This is a build-and-run walkthrough of **norviq**, an open-source runtime Policy Enforcement/Decision Point that intercepts every agent tool call in a Kubernetes cluster and returns allow / block / escalate / audit, evaluated against OPA/Rego policy plus behavioral trust.  I'll show the architecture — a sidecar/SDK PEP and a central PDP — and how the policy contract maps to the OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS: prompt injection, data leakage, excessive agency, cross-tenant access, chain-depth limits, with evasion-normalized matching that defeats homoglyph and base64 tricks. You'll see an attack graph that maps how an agent could reach a crown-jewel data source through its tools, and a red-team suite that scores which attacks actually block — so "secure" is a number, not a claim.  Then the DevSecOps parts that decide whether it survives production: keeping the enforcement path fail-closed everywhere (and the two places it quietly failed open), why a short decision cache is a security control, self-asserted vs cryptographically attested identity, and rolling enforcement out in a monitor mode so teams can measure before they block.  norviq is open source — pip-installable, with a Helm chart on Artifact Hub, and independently pen-tested — so this is field experience, not slideware. You'll leave with a concrete pattern for governing what your agents do, not just what they say.

Title: AI Agents for DevSecOps: Automating Secure Infrastructure, Delivery, and Incident Response
Abstract: DevSecOps teams are responsible for Infrastructure as Code, CI/CD security, Kubernetes governance, vulnerability management, observability, compliance, reliability, and incident response. Yet many organizations still depend on engineers to manually review alerts, validate configurations, investigate deployment failures, inspect security findings, and execute operational runbooks.  This session explores how AI agents powered by Large Language Models can act as intelligent orchestration layers across the DevSecOps lifecycle. Using the Model Context Protocol, agents can securely interact with Terraform, Kubernetes, GitHub, GitOps pipelines, AWS, Azure, OCI, Splunk, Grafana, CloudWatch, PagerDuty, ServiceNow, security scanners, internal documentation, and approved runbooks.  The presentation demonstrates how AI agents can generate and validate Infrastructure as Code, enforce security policies, review pull requests, identify configuration drift, analyze vulnerabilities, verify deployments, correlate telemetry, and assist with incident investigation. A reusable investigation workflow follows a structured 16-step process that includes retrieving incident context, analyzing logs and metrics, reviewing recent code and infrastructure changes, identifying probable root causes, recommending remediation, and escalating high-risk decisions for human approval.  The session also examines essential guardrails, including least-privilege access, policy-as-code, approval gates, audit trails, restricted tool permissions, and human-in-the-loop controls. These safeguards help ensure that AI-assisted automation remains secure, explainable, and compliant.  Attendees will learn how AI agents can reduce DevSecOps toil, accelerate secure delivery, improve policy enforcement, strengthen incident response, and enable engineering teams to focus on resilience, architecture, and continuous security improvement.

Title: When AI Ignores the Deny List
Abstract: Claude Code ships a permissions.deny system in settings.json meant to block agents from touching sensitive files. In practice, deny rules can be silently bypassed - an agent asked to read .env may just read it, permissions notwithstanding. This talk walks through that gap, why it matters once agents run inside CI/CD or with elevated file access, and the practical mitigation: PreToolUse hooks that intercept tool calls before execution and enforce policy in your own code, not the model's. I'll cover the settings.json hierarchy (user/project/local), where policy actually lives, what a working hook-based guardrail looks like, and what a pentest of an AI-built or AI-operated app should specifically check for. Attendees leave with a settings.json + hook template they can drop into any Claude Code project today.

Title: Your SBOM Stops at the model
Abstract: DevSecOps got good at a specific problem: proving what is in the artifact. Scan it, sign it, generate an SBOM, gate the pipeline on provenance. That entire apparatus assumes the artifact is code you can read.  Then the artifact started carrying weights. A model-bearing service ships a multi-gigabyte binary blob that no scanner parses, that no SBOM format meaningfully describes, and whose behavior is not a function of its source. This talk is about the specific places a working DevSecOps pipeline goes quiet when an agent moves through it. I will cover which gates still fire, which ones pass an artifact they cannot actually inspect, and what a security engineer should ask for instead. When I keynoted CloudNativeSecurityCon in 2023, the number I put on the stage was six of every seven: six of every seven project vulnerabilities are inherited from dependencies nobody on the team wrote. This is the first one you cannot read at all.

Title: Shifting Left on LLM Security: Detecting and Preventing Data Leakage in Your AI Pipeline
Abstract: As organizations integrate Large Language Models into their software delivery pipelines, a new class of security risk emerges: models that inadvertently memorize and regurgitate sensitive training data, exposing PII, proprietary code, and confidential documents through their outputs. For DevSecOps teams, this isn't just an AI problem — it's a pipeline problem that demands the same shift-left discipline applied to traditional application security.  This session examines the mechanisms behind LLM data leakage and extraction, and shows how these risks can be treated as a security gate within existing CI/CD and MLOps workflows rather than an afterthought discovered post-deployment. Attendees will learn practical detection techniques for auditing model outputs, including automated scanning approaches that can be embedded into build and deployment pipelines to flag sensitive or confidential content before it reaches production.  The talk will cover how to build continuous auditing processes for LLM outputs, integrate data-leakage checks alongside existing SAST/DAST tooling, and establish governance guardrails that scale with model usage across teams. The goal is to give DevSecOps practitioners a concrete playbook for evaluating LLM safety pre-deployment and embedding responsible AI controls directly into the software supply chain  turning AI governance from a compliance checkbox into an automated, repeatable pipeline practice.

Title: When AI Joins the Request Path: Securing API-Backed AI Systems
Abstract: AI-backed APIs introduce new security and reliability risks because a single request may now trigger model inference, retrieve user context, call internal services, rank personalized content, or invoke downstream tools. Traditional API security controls still matter, but they are not enough when the system includes probabilistic outputs, dynamic context injection, automated decisioning, and fallback behavior inside a latency-sensitive path. This session examines practical DevSecOps patterns for securing AI-backed APIs in production. We will look at threat boundaries around user input, retrieved context, feature pipelines, model calls, authorization, logging, audit trails, rate limiting, prompt or tool misuse, and downstream service access. The focus is not abstract AI risk; it is the engineering work needed to make AI-enabled request flows safer to build, deploy, monitor, and operate. Attendees will leave with a practical checklist: what to validate at API boundaries, where to place authorization checks, what to log and what not to log, how to minimize sensitive data exposure, how to design safer fallback behavior, and which observability signals help detect abuse, degradation, or unsafe model behavior before it becomes an incident.

Title: Secure Enterprise RAG: Building Trusted Vectorized Knowledge Systems for DevSecOps
Abstract: Modern DevSecOps environments generate large volumes of documentation, operational knowledge, security artifacts, and deployment data that must be accessible without compromising governance or trust. Traditional keyword-based search often fails to retrieve relevant information across these distributed knowledge sources, limiting operational efficiency and slowing incident response. This session explores how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and vectorized knowledge architectures enable secure, production-ready enterprise knowledge platforms for modern engineering organizations.  The presentation examines practical architectural patterns for building enterprise RAG systems, including document ingestion, embedding generation, vector indexing, hybrid retrieval, and context-aware response generation. It discusses how security controls, identity-aware access, encryption, governance policies, and auditability can be integrated throughout the retrieval pipeline to protect sensitive enterprise knowledge while improving developer productivity. The session also covers techniques for reducing hallucinations through grounded retrieval, trusted data sources, retrieval evaluation, and human oversight.  Drawing from enterprise architecture practices and production implementation patterns, the presentation highlights lessons learned in designing scalable, cloud-native AI knowledge systems that support engineering, operations, and security teams. Emerging approaches such as agentic workflows and graph-enhanced retrieval are also discussed to demonstrate how organizations can improve reasoning across complex information ecosystems. Attendees will leave with practical guidance for designing secure, trustworthy, and operationally resilient AI knowledge platforms that align with DevSecOps principles.

JobTitle1: Senior Staff Software Engineer, Enterprise Architecture and AI
Title: LLM Guardrails for Enterprise Audit: Patterns Beyond Toy Filters
Abstract: Enterprise LLM applications need guardrails that survive compliance review. This talk covers production guardrail patterns using NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, and Llama Guard; how to handle PII with Microsoft Presidio; prompt-injection defenses that actually work against indirect attacks; and the policy-as-code patterns that connect guardrails to enterprise governance frameworks such as the EU AI Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.  Takeaways: A guardrail-stack reference. PII engineering patterns for LLM pipelines. Defenses against indirect prompt injection. A policy-as-code approach to AI governance.  Audience: security engineers, platform engineers, AI engineers. Level: Intermediate to advanced.

Title: Cell-Based Isolation for Multi-Tenant Platforms on Kubernetes
Abstract: Namespaces and NetworkPolicies are usually where multi-tenant Kubernetes isolation stops, that's good enough to stop accidents, not good enough to stop a determined neighbor. This talk walks through the cell-based architecture we built into OpenChoreo, an open-source Internal Developer Platform and a CNCF Sandbox project, where every tenant's environment gets its own cell: a namespace bound to a Cilium (eBPF) network policy boundary and its own observability scope, with traffic entering and leaving only through explicitly directional gateways.  We'll break down the four traffic directions: northbound (public ingress), westbound (org-internal ingress), southbound (egress to external services), and eastbound (org-internal egress) and show how each is enforced with Cilium and an Envoy-based Kubernetes Gateway API implementation.  You'll leave with a concrete pattern for reasoning about tenant blast radius on Kubernetes: what a cell boundary actually stops, what it doesn't, where RBAC/ABAC needs to pick up where network isolation ends, and the tradeoffs we hit running this in production across single-cluster and multi-cluster topologies.  Key takeaways:  - A practical model (cells + directional gateways) for reasoning about tenant blast radius on Kubernetes, beyond "namespace + NetworkPolicy" - How to enforce egress-side controls (credential injection, circuit breaking, quotas) as a first-class part of tenant isolation, not an afterthought - Where network-layer isolation stops and RBAC/ABAC needs to take over - Real tradeoffs from running this across single-cluster and multi-cluster deployment topologies

Title: Anti-Entropy Mechanisms for Single-Digit Minute Latency in Cloud-Scale Security Platforms
Abstract: Cloud providers now generate continuous streams of vulnerability findings across globally distributed infrastructure, and every minute of delay in delivering a finding widens the window of exposure for the government agencies, financial institutions, and healthcare systems that depend on that infrastructure. Distributed platforms responsible for this delivery face a classic tension, formalized by the CAP theorem, between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, making single-digit-minute delivery difficult to reconcile with correctness at cloud scale. This talk presents an architecture that resolves that tension by adapting anti-entropy patterns from distributed database research, including Merkle-tree comparison, read-repair, and hinted handoff, into a security-specific reconciliation layer. Findings are enriched with severity and asset context, then reconciled through priority-aware, attribute-level hashing that captures not just missing data but silent corruption of existing findings. Paired with a streaming-first ingestion layer, this anti-entropy backstop delivers the vast majority of findings within seconds and closes the remaining gap within single-digit minutes, all while preserving an audit-compliant record of every repair. Attendees, including platform architects, security engineers, and engineering leaders, will leave with concrete, transferable patterns for designing distributed systems that must reconcile speed, correctness, and scale under real-world failure conditions.

Title: Building Resilient Cloud Native Security Through DevSecOps and Continuous Compliance
Abstract: As organizations accelerate cloud native adoption, security can no longer be a downstream concern. It must be embedded across every stage of the software development lifecycle. This session presents a practical, experience-driven approach to building resilient cloud security by integrating DevSecOps practices from code commit to production.  Drawing from real-world implementations across cloud and application ecosystems at enterprise scale, this talk walks through how security controls can be embedded at every layer: code security, container security, Kubernetes security, API protection, configuration governance, dependency management, runtime protection, and continuous compliance.  Attendees will see how shift-left security mechanisms, including pre-commit secret detection, static code analysis, dependency scanning, image vulnerability assessment, image signing, and dynamic application security testing, can proactively eliminate risk before it reaches production. The session covers practical tooling across SonarQube, Black Duck, OWASP ZAP, Prisma Cloud, Amazon GuardDuty, CrowdStrike, Tenable, and Cloud Custodian in hybrid and multi-cloud environments.  A dedicated segment covers Kubernetes and platform security: network policies, RBAC, audit logging, secrets management, mutual TLS, and runtime monitoring. The session also addresses modern threat vectors, including insider threats, cloud misconfigurations, software supply chain risks, and evolving cyber adversaries.  Security leaders, cloud architects, DevOps engineers, and platform teams will leave with actionable strategies to build a security-first culture that accelerates innovation, strengthens operational resilience, and supports continuous compliance in cloud-powered digital transformation.

Title: Terraform for Secure Multi-Cloud DevSecOps: Automating Scalable Infrastructure as Code
Abstract: Managing secure infrastructure consistently across multiple cloud providers is a fundamental challenge for modern DevSecOps teams. As organizations accelerate cloud adoption, infrastructure automation must balance deployment speed, security, governance, and operational reliability without introducing unnecessary complexity. This session demonstrates how Terraform provides a practical foundation for building secure, scalable, and repeatable Infrastructure as Code workflows across heterogeneous cloud environments. Attendees will explore provider-agnostic architecture patterns, modular Terraform design, remote state management, automated provisioning, and CI/CD integration that enable engineering teams to standardize infrastructure delivery while reducing manual intervention. The presentation also examines practical security controls, including policy-as-code, secrets management, identity and access governance, compliance automation, and continuous infrastructure validation, showing how security can be integrated directly into deployment pipelines rather than treated as a separate process. Drawing on enterprise cloud implementations, the discussion shares lessons learned from designing resilient multi-cloud platforms, improving deployment consistency, strengthening operational governance, and simplifying large-scale infrastructure management. Additional focus is given to monitoring, automated drift detection, infrastructure testing, and operational observability to support continuous improvement throughout the infrastructure lifecycle. Attendees will leave with practical patterns, implementation guidance, and operational insights for building secure, automated multi-cloud platforms that strengthen DevSecOps practices while accelerating software delivery and improving long-term infrastructure reliability.

Title: Secretless Multi-Cloud Authentication with Workload Identity for DevSecOps Pipelines
Abstract: Multi-cloud DevSecOps pipelines frequently move application data, artifacts, and machine learning workloads across provider boundaries, creating security challenges when persistent credentials are embedded in automation. This talk presents a policy-driven approach to secretless multi-cloud authentication using OpenID Connect and workload identity federation to replace long-lived service keys with short-lived, runtime-issued identity assertions. The architecture enables automated data integration between heterogeneous cloud environments while reducing credential exposure and simplifying operational security controls. The session examines how federated workload identities can be incorporated into event-driven pipelines without introducing unnecessary authentication overhead or disrupting high-throughput data movement. It also explores practical design considerations for policy enforcement, identity trust relationships, credential lifecycle management, observability, failure handling, and secure automation across distributed environments. A mathematical model is used to illustrate how reducing credential lifetime changes the persistent-key vulnerability surface as pipeline concurrency increases. The proposed framework removes persistent credential files from cross-cloud workflows and demonstrated more than a 90 percent reduction in persistent credential attack surface while supporting low-latency MLOps data ingestion. Attendees will learn practical patterns for designing secretless CI/CD and data pipelines, applying least-privilege workload identity, and integrating security controls directly into DevSecOps automation without sacrificing scalability, reliability, or developer productivity.

Title: Building ML-Based Compliance Monitoring for Automated Risk Detection
Abstract: Modern engineering teams are increasingly adopting automation and intelligent systems to improve operational reliability, security, and governance. However, managing compliance risks across global workforce operations remains challenging when organizations rely on manual reviews and fragmented monitoring processes.  This session shares a real-world case study of building and deploying a Machine Learning-powered Working Hours Alert System (WHAS) to automate compliance monitoring and detect potential time fraud risks. The solution continuously analyzes time and attendance data, identifies unusual working-hour patterns, generates actionable alerts, and supports proactive responses aligned with labor regulations and organizational policies.  The presentation will cover the engineering considerations behind implementing an AI-driven monitoring solution, including data analysis approaches, anomaly detection strategies, alert design, system integration, and maintaining transparency through human oversight. It will also highlight lessons learned from introducing automation into an enterprise compliance workflow, including challenges, design decisions, and operational improvements.  Attendees will gain practical insights into how machine learning can be applied to build scalable risk detection systems that improve governance, reduce manual effort, and strengthen operational processes. This session demonstrates how automation and intelligent monitoring can help teams create more reliable, secure, and efficient enterprise workflows.

Title: Building Security Into the Upgrade Pipeline: Escaping Vendor-Managed Risk
Abstract: When a third-party vendor owns your patch cycle, you don't control your own exposure window — and no amount of downstream security tooling fixes that. This talk covers how we moved GRC platform upgrades from vendor-dependent to internally owned, without sacrificing stability or compliance.  The core of it was building security and validation directly into the upgrade pipeline: architectural decoupling to remove vendor bottlenecks, standardized upgrade methodology, and automated pre-upgrade testing, post-upgrade verification, and continuous monitoring the same practices that make CI/CD pipelines trustworthy, applied to infrastructure upgrades that used to be a vendor's black box.  Production results: 30–45% less vulnerability exposure, 40–50% fewer system failures, 60% fewer configuration errors, upgrade timelines cut in half, and 70–90% less vendor dependency.  This is a practical walkthrough for teams who inherited vendor-managed infrastructure and want to bring security ownership in-house without breaking what already works what to decouple first, how to validate safely, and what monitoring actually needs to catch.

Title: AI-Driven Sensitive Data Discovery for Secure DevSecOps and Privacy Compliance
Abstract: Modern DevSecOps environments rarely keep sensitive data in one place. Enterprise applications distribute regulated information across cloud services, APIs, operational databases, analytics platforms, logs, and hybrid infrastructure, making manual discovery and periodic compliance reviews difficult to sustain. This session presents a practical approach to AI-driven sensitive data discovery that integrates metadata intelligence, semantic analysis, runtime telemetry, and automated governance workflows into modern DevSecOps practices.  The presentation explores, through practical engineering scenarios, how engineering teams can design discovery pipelines that continuously identify sensitive data, classify risk, and surface compliance issues as systems change. It examines practical architecture and design choices for combining machine learning with deterministic policies, metadata signals, application context, and operational telemetry, while addressing challenges such as false positives, explainability, changing schemas, and distributed ownership. The session also covers how discovery findings can trigger automated workflows for validation, remediation, and evidence collection, connecting security and privacy controls with everyday DevSecOps processes.  Attendees will gain practical, reusable patterns for building continuous sensitive-data visibility, integrating discovery into delivery and operational workflows, and improving privacy risk detection without relying solely on manual audits. The session ultimately concludes with lessons for evolving toward intelligent, automated governance and stronger operational resilience across distributed systems.

Title: Trust but Verify: Catching Data Masking Failures Before Test Data Ships  Talk Type or Format:
Abstract: Data masking validation is straightforward when every source and target row shares a stable primary key. Enterprise systems rarely cooperate. Legacy databases, migrated tables, and append-only logs may lack reliable keys, while creating composite keys across hundreds of millions of rows can be prohibitively expensive.  This session presents an architecture that narrows the problem before performing row-level comparison. The method first intersects sensitive values between source and masked target datasets, isolates only the overlapping candidates, accounts for the different behavior of random and dictionary-based replacement, and generates stable composite identifiers only for the narrowed subset.  This makes it possible to distinguish actual masking failures from legitimate dictionary-replacement collisions without generating keys for the entire dataset.  The session walks through the complete decision tree, SQL-oriented examples, architectural tradeoffs, and important limitations such as duplicate candidates and composite-key stability. Attendees will learn how to design a scalable validation layer that preserves evidence, reduces unnecessary computation, and supports repeatable privacy checks in complex test-data environments.

JobTitle1: Senior Manager of Data Engineering and Analytics
Title: Securing Real Time Mobile Analytics: Identity Binding and Low Latency Authorization for Distributed Enterprise Data
Abstract: Operational leaders, including plant managers, regional directors, and executives, increasingly access enterprise analytics from unmanaged personal mobile devices rather than corporate laptops, a shift that expands the attack surface long before any dashboard renders. This session presents the security architecture required to deliver real time analytics safely to a mobile first audience across a distributed enterprise spanning multiple facilities and business domains.  The talk covers how enterprise identity binding is enforced on unmanaged devices, ensuring that a personal phone accessing operational data carries the same trust guarantees as a managed corporate endpoint. It examines role based authorization resolved through cached permission checks, a design that must balance the strict access control mobile and BYOD contexts demand against the response time users expect, since a slow authorization check on mobile is felt far more acutely than on desktop.  A central challenge addressed is securing cross domain data integration, reconciling manufacturing, sales, service, and workforce data, each governed by its own source system and access policy, into a single mobile experience without creating gaps in the permission model during multi level drill down from enterprise summary to individual shift. The session also covers how minute level data freshness sourced from a distributed warehouse architecture is kept consistent with access control at every refresh, so speed never comes at the cost of a stale or incorrectly scoped permission state.  Finally, the talk looks at the security implications of push based, AI augmented insight delivery and natural language querying on mobile, where extending conversational, retrieval augmented access to operational data introduces new questions around query scoped authorization and data exposure. Attendees will leave with a concrete blueprint for building mobile analytics platforms where identity, access control, and low latency performance are treated as one design problem rather than three separate concerns.

Title: DevSecOps for Cloud Migration: Securing Data Integration Across Enterprise Platforms
Abstract: As organizations accelerate cloud adoption, securing data integration and migration workflows has become a critical challenge for DevSecOps teams. This session presents a practical framework for implementing secure cloud migration and enterprise data integration pipelines while maintaining compliance, reliability, and operational efficiency. Drawing from real-world deployments across healthcare, education, and public-sector environments, the talk explores how Infrastructure as Code (IaC), policy-as-code, automated security testing, and continuous compliance validation can be embedded throughout the software delivery lifecycle. Attendees will learn how cloud-native architectures leverage CI/CD pipelines, container security scanning, secrets management, runtime protection, and observability platforms to reduce deployment risk while improving system resilience. The session also examines the role of centralized logging, automated remediation workflows, and governance controls in managing large-scale cloud migrations involving sensitive data and distributed workloads. Performance results from enterprise implementations demonstrate reductions in operational overhead, improved deployment consistency, faster release cycles, and enhanced security posture through integrated DevSecOps practices. Practical lessons learned, architectural trade-offs, implementation challenges, and recommendations for securing modern cloud ecosystems will be shared. Participants will leave with actionable strategies for building scalable, compliant, and secure cloud migration programs that align development velocity with enterprise security and governance requirements.

Title: Securing the AI Perimeter: Building Zero-Trust Integration Patterns for AI-Driven Pricing in SAP
Abstract: Enterprises racing to embed AI into core financial systems face a hard constraint: innovation cannot come at the cost of system integrity, auditability, or financial control. Pricing engines sit inside the Order-to-Cash pipeline, and any external AI integration must be secured, governed, and clean-core compliant from day one — not retrofitted after a breach or an audit failure.  This session presents a production-tested architecture for securely integrating an external AI pricing engine with enterprise SAP systems, built around a hard security boundary: SAP retains sole authority over transactional consistency and financial validation, while the AI engine is confined to a stateless recommendation role with no write access to core financial objects. Integration is implemented through HTTP-based APIs and SAP BAdI extension points, with zero modification to standard SAP objects  preserving upgrade safety, auditability, and a minimal attack surface by design.  We walk through the DevSecOps practices that made this deployment safe to ship: securing and rate-limiting the AI-to-SAP API boundary, validating and sanitizing every model output before it touches a financial transaction, enforcing least-privilege access between the AI layer and SAP, and building in circuit breakers and rollback paths so a misbehaving model can never directly alter pricing, discounting, or revenue data. We also cover the governance layer: logging and traceability for every AI-influenced pricing decision, to satisfy internal audit and regulatory review.  Attendees will leave with a concrete blueprint for threat-modeling AI integrations into core ERP systems, practical ABAP-side guardrail patterns, and a replicable security architecture for teams under pressure to adopt AI without compromising the financial controls their business depends on.

Title: Shifting Left with AI: Building Security and Compliance-by-Design into CRM and ERP Pipelines
Abstract: AI is turning CRM and ERP platforms into autonomous, decision-making systems—and every model, API, and data pipeline behind that autonomy is a new attack surface most DevSecOps practices weren't built to handle. As AI-driven CRM adoption grows toward a $51.5 billion market by 2028 and AI-enabled ERP toward $123.41 billion by 2029, security and compliance teams are being asked to secure systems that increasingly make decisions on their own, at machine speed.  This talk applies DevSecOps principles directly to AI-powered CRM and ERP environments. We'll walk through securing the ML pipelines and data flows behind automated lead scoring and customer service workflows, locking down API access and secrets for AI agents integrated into ERP financial and inventory systems, and building automated compliance gates into CI/CD pipelines to meet requirements like the EU AI Act before code ever reaches production.  We'll also cover phased, security-gated rollout patterns that reduce production incidents, and how "compliance-by-design"—checks embedded directly into the pipeline rather than bolted on after deployment—has cut remediation costs by roughly 70% in real implementations. Drawing on examples from financial services, manufacturing, retail, and healthcare, attendees will leave with concrete patterns for securing the AI-driven CRM and ERP systems their organizations are already shipping.

Title: Securing the AI Pipeline: DevSecOps Strategies for AI-Driven HR and Finance Systems
Abstract: AI is now embedded deep inside the enterprise systems that handle an organization's most sensitive data: employee records, compensation, financial transactions, and compliance-critical reporting. Yet most DevSecOps practices haven't caught up to the unique security surface these AI-driven HR and Finance systems introduce. This session presents a practical framework for shifting security and compliance left into the AI development lifecycle for these high-risk domains, drawing on empirical research and enterprise implementation patterns.  On the talent and workforce side, AI-driven recruitment and predictive workforce platforms ingest and infer highly sensitive personal data, creating new attack surfaces and privacy exposure that traditional AppSec pipelines weren't built to catch. This session covers threat modeling for AI-driven HR pipelines, data minimization and access-control patterns for PII-heavy training data, and continuous validation approaches for detecting model drift that could silently reintroduce bias or leakage.  In financial operations, machine learning-powered accounting, reconciliation, and anomaly-detection systems are increasingly the last line of defense against fraud and compliance violations, which makes their own integrity a security-critical concern. We'll examine how to build security and audit controls directly into the CI/CD pipelines for these models: securing training data provenance, testing for adversarial manipulation of fraud-detection models, and embedding explainability checks as automated gates rather than after-the-fact audits.  Technology alone doesn't close the gap. Algorithmic bias, data privacy, and model explainability are now security and compliance failure modes, not just ethical concerns, and this session addresses concrete governance-as-code strategies teams can implement at any AI maturity stage. Attendees will leave with a tiered roadmap for integrating security, privacy, and compliance controls into AI-driven HR and Finance systems, from foundational data governance to fully automated, policy-as-code enforcement across the AI SDLC.

Title: Building AI-Native DevSecOps Platforms with Governed Platform Engineering
Abstract: Modern platform teams face a dual challenge: building secure infrastructure that supports AI applications while embedding AI into DevSecOps workflows to improve delivery, operations, and security. This session presents a practical reference architecture that unifies both objectives through governance, automation, and observability, enabling organizations to adopt AI without compromising reliability, security, or operational control.  The presentation explores how platform engineering evolves to support retrieval-augmented generation, inference services, intelligent agents, and model lifecycle management alongside traditional cloud-native workloads. It examines production-ready practices for integrating policy-as-code, zero-trust security, model provenance, auditability, role-based access control, and continuous observability into AI-enabled platforms. The session also demonstrates how governed AI agents can automate deployment validation, incident response, self-healing, operational remediation, and compliance while maintaining human oversight through approval gates and measurable policies. Using real-world platform engineering experiences, attendees will gain actionable guidance for designing secure, scalable, and resilient AI-powered DevSecOps platforms that combine automation with governance. The discussion concludes with practical lessons on balancing innovation, operational safety, and security while preparing engineering organizations for the next generation of autonomous software delivery and intelligent cloud operations.

Title: How Enterprise AI Systems Delivered $30M ROI Through Security Automation
Abstract: Enterprise AI adoption is accelerating, but many organizations struggle to move beyond pilots into secure, scalable, and operationally sustainable production systems. This session presents lessons learned from building and operating six enterprise AI platforms that generated more than $30.4 million in documented financial impact across retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), autonomous AI agents, intelligent document processing, cloud optimization, and security automation.  Built across globally distributed infrastructure supporting 270 data centers and more than 10,000 customers, these systems required balancing AI innovation with governance, reliability, cost control, and security. This talk focuses on the architectural decisions, operational challenges, and automation strategies that enabled successful production deployment at scale.  Attendees will learn how tiered model routing reduced AI inference costs by 74% while maintaining 94% response accuracy, how intelligent document processing achieved a 35:1 ROI, and how autonomous remediation systems reduced operational triage workloads by 67% while automatically resolving more than 35,000 vulnerabilities. The session also covers the practical implementation of an Enterprise AI FinOps framework focused on visibility, allocation, optimization, and governance.  Beyond the successes, the presentation highlights key lessons learned around AI cost management, multi-cloud operations, security automation, and production governance. Attendees will gain practical approaches for measuring AI value, reducing operational overhead, improving security response workflows, and deploying AI systems that remain both financially accountable and operationally reliable.  This session is intended for DevSecOps engineers, platform teams, architects, security practitioners, and technology leaders looking for real-world guidance on building and operating enterprise AI systems that deliver measurable business outcomes while improving security and operational efficiency.

Title: Would Your Alert Have Fired in Time? Grading Detection Rules Against 46 Real Exploits
Abstract: Teams ship detection rules constantly, but very few can verify whether an alert will fire early enough to prevent a total loss. This talk breaks down a testing methodology and simulation harness built to replay candidate detection rules against 46 historical exploit events using state-forked execution and archive-node data streams.  We will cover:  Replay Architecture: Rebuilding incidents block-by-block to evaluate detector precision and real-time responsiveness.  Time-to-Detect Metrics: Deriving empirical detection deadlines based on observed exfiltration curves rather than arbitrary SLAs.  False-Positive Budgeting: Managing detector precision when automated mitigation involves irreversible circuit breakers and protocol pauses.  Private Mempool Coverage: Addressing critical telemetry blind spots caused by zero-visibility private transaction routing.  The talk includes a live walk-through and open-source release of the replay harness. While grounded in public Web3 exploit data, the evaluation architecture, metric scoring, and testing frameworks apply directly to any cloud-native DevSecOps alerting pipeline.

Title: AI-Driven Autohealing and Intelligent Observability for Cloud-Native DevSecOps Platforms
Abstract: Modern DevSecOps environments rely on cloud-native microservices that continuously evolve through automated delivery pipelines, making operational resilience a critical engineering objective. As application complexity increases, conventional rule-based monitoring often struggles to detect correlated failures across distributed systems, delaying recovery and increasing operational risk. This session presents a practical approach to building AI-driven autohealing capabilities by combining metrics, distributed traces, logs, and event streams into a unified observability architecture that enables intelligent fault detection and adaptive recovery.  Attendees will explore how machine learning models identify abnormal system behavior, correlate telemetry across services, localize probable root causes, and initiate automated remediation through Kubernetes orchestration. The session discusses the implementation of closed-loop recovery workflows, confidence-based automation, and governance mechanisms that ensure autonomous actions remain transparent, auditable, and aligned with operational security practices. Practical deployment considerations, lessons learned from production environments, and strategies for safely introducing adaptive automation into DevSecOps workflows are also covered.  The presentation demonstrates how intelligent observability and AI-assisted recovery improve operational reliability while reducing alert fatigue and accelerating incident response. Real-world implementations show that AI-driven autohealing can reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR) by 40–70%, correlated observability can reduce diagnosis time by 50–65%, and learned behavioral baselines can lower false-positive alert rates by 60% or more. Participants will leave with actionable architectural patterns for building resilient, secure, and self-healing cloud-native platforms.

Title: Deterministic Kubernetes Diagnostics with OpenTelemetry for Secure DevSecOps Operations
Abstract: Distributed enterprise platforms running on Kubernetes can make request failures difficult to diagnose when telemetry is fragmented across services, logs, metrics, and tracing systems. This session presents a practical approach to building deterministic request-level diagnostics using OpenTelemetry and the W3C Trace Context standard. Rather than treating observability as isolated instrumentation work, the session examines the architecture and engineering decisions required to make request tracing reliable, secure, and operationally useful across independently deployed microservices. The approach combines ingress-level trace identity, mandatory context propagation, allowlist-based metadata, configuration-driven telemetry controls, and non-disruptive handling of telemetry failures. The session draws on a production enterprise platform to explain implementation lessons, including how architectural constraints, security requirements, and failure scenarios shaped the final design. It introduces seven independently testable evaluation criteria for verifying tracing completeness and operational readiness, while capturing nine approved operational trace metadata fields through an allowlist model. The design maintains zero request impact when telemetry components fail and supports enterprise compliance requirements including SOC 2, HIPAA, and PCI-DSS. Attendees will gain practical techniques for debugging distributed Kubernetes systems, improving observability reliability, reducing diagnostic friction, and integrating security and resilience into DevSecOps workflows.

Title: Recovery Without Reintroducing Risk: A Security-First Approach to RTO/RPO in Event-Driven Systems
Abstract: Recovery time and data-loss targets tell you a system came back online — they don't tell you whether it came back safe. In event-driven systems, a recovery that meets RTO and RPO can still replay duplicate events, restore stale authorization state, invert message ordering, or leave joins incomplete — each of which is not just a correctness gap but a security exposure: replayed transactions that bypass fraud controls, stale permission or session state that grants access it shouldn't, or partial writes that leave audit trails inconsistent. Conventional recovery metrics don't capture this class of risk, which means teams can pass their resilience benchmarks while quietly reintroducing security and compliance failures during the very process meant to restore trust in the system.  This session introduces the Semantic Recovery Envelope, a framework for evaluating the security and correctness posture of a recovery response before it's executed. The Envelope examines duplication, staleness, ordering, and join completeness as risk dimensions, and uses that evaluation to select the response  replay, rollback, compensation, partial service, or traffic isolation  that restores service without reopening an attack surface or violating a compliance boundary.  The presentation walks through how these decisions hold up under real operating conditions, including regional failover, incomplete downstream writes, and partial infrastructure failures, and how teams can build evidence-backed confidence  the kind auditors and security reviewers ask for  that a chosen recovery path restores not just uptime, but integrity.  Attendees, including DevSecOps engineers, SRE and platform security leads, and real-time data processing practitioners, will gain a practical approach for defining security-aware recovery objectives alongside RTO and RPO, a structured way to reason about recovery strategy selection without creating new risk, and validation techniques that hold up to security review in event-driven and stateful architectures across cloud and infrastructure environments.

Title: DevSecOps beyond GitHub Advanced Security
Abstract: DevSecOps tries to make DevOps teams aware about integrating security into each and every step of the process. But this is complex, with a need to integrate a whole set of tools. But no more, thanks to GitHub Advanced Security, baked into your trusted DevOps environment. In this session, Peter will guide you through a full range of built-in GitHub security features, beyond the GHAS - GitHub Advanced Security plan you (might) already pay for.

Title: When Working JavaScript Breaks: Browser Security Policies in Practice
Abstract: In this talk, we will examine how browser security policies break JavaScript execution and leave with concrete strategies for catching and fixing these issues early in development. We'll start with live demos of how browser security policies break common JavaScript patterns, then look at ways to catch these issues earlier.  It is based on my real life experience working on a web SDK that customers embed into their site: code that worked correctly in my environment would suddenly break once added into a customer's site, because they used different security headers, like Content Security Policy (CSP) or Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP).  We’ll look at demos of how browser security policies block eval and blob-based resources, change the way iframe can communicate with parent windows, and break popups.  Once we've seen how these policies break things, we'll look at how to catch these issues earlier in development. Checking source code and build output can help us find capabilities that will be blocked by security headers, automated testing - demonstrate how our code actually works under browser constraints, and report-only policies - try out security headers without breaking our sites.  The goal is to help developers treat security policies as part of the development process and catch possible issues earlier.

Title: Verification Timing: Why Checking AI-Written Code at the Gate Is Already Too Late
Abstract:
Security gates were designed around a human pace. Someone writes code, opens a pull request, and a scanner or a reviewer inspects what arrived. That model quietly assumed the volume of code reaching the gate was bounded by how fast people type.

AI coding agents broke that assumption. They run unattended for hours, produce more change than any gate can meaningfully inspect, and they routinely break code they had already gotten working. In CoderCup, a public competition where four frontier coding agents built the same ten-phase application under identical rules, every agent broke previously working features between 31 and 57 times during a single build. Those breaks stayed invisible until something actually ran the application.

This talk is about verification timing. Not whether to verify, but when. Across CoderCup, agents got the task right on the first attempt about 80% of the time and reached 94% once a verification loop caught the failure and drove the fix. That gain happened inside the agent's own loop, before anything reached a pipeline. Verification that runs only at the gate arrives after the mess is already made. Give the agent those same checks while it works, so it finds each break and fixes each one before moving on.

Attendees will leave with a way to think about where verification belongs in an agent-driven pipeline, which two numbers are worth putting on a dashboard, and what evidence to demand from any tool claiming to check an agent's work.

Title: Making AIOps safe for production
Abstract: The era of writing every infrastructure configuration script by hand is ending. New AIOps tools and AI-assisted platforms can now instantly generate complex Chef recipes, Terraform modules, and shell scripts, directly ingesting them into our DevOps systems for execution. The speed is phenomenal, but the risk is unprecedented. What happens when an AI hallucination—or a subtly malicious prompt injection—instructs your pipeline to drop a database, revoke critical IAM permissions, or misconfigure a load balancer?  This talk is a survival guide for the modern DevOps and SRE practitioner. I will share hard-won experiences from the trenches of integrating agentic AIOps tools with enterprise infrastructure as code (IaC) like Chef. We will break down the exact architectural safeguards required to keep your production environment secure when AI is writing the code.  First, we will dive into automated validation pipelines. You will learn how to implement strict static analysis, linting, and security checks on AI-generated bash, PowerShell, and Ruby before it ever executes. Second, we will discuss the absolute necessity of high-fidelity test environments. If AI is generating the scripts, your staging environment must be a perfect, matched clone of production where these scripts can be safely “detonated” and validated.  Finally, we will examine the paradigm shift in orchestration: the Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Gatekeeper. We will explore how to design agentic workflows that pause execution for high-risk changes, elevating the DevOps engineer into a safety “approver” role. We aren’t being replaced by AI; our jobs are evolving. Join me to learn how to step up from writing the scripts to orchestrating the agents.  More at https://www.papercall.io/talks/436070

Title: A Superscript One Walks Past the Guard: Six Byte-Level Escapes in Reviewed Code
Abstract: An agent asks its HTTP tool to fetch 0.¹.0.0. The egress allowlist standing in front of that tool agrees that string is not an IP address, so the request goes through. UTS-46 mapping then folds U+00B9 down to U+0031, and the socket opens to 0.1.0.0, the address the allowlist exists to refuse. I run that live, offline, against a listener on a laptop, and the whole proof of concept is one line long.  Nothing malfunctioned. The guard and the runtime read one request as two different byte strings, and inside a CI pipeline, a policy engine, or an agent tool runtime, that gap is architecture rather than accident. Each of those things inspects input at some distance from whatever finally acts on it. Check ahead of a transform and the transform changes what you approved. Check after a decode and the decode has thrown away the thing you needed to look at.  I have hit this six times in reviewed code, twice in code of my own, and the recurrences do not resemble each other until you line them up. A vocabulary-safety check passed a label because what it inspected was a decoded string, while the bytes underneath were ill-formed CESU-8 that a lenient decoder had substituted long before the check ran. Elsewhere, five implementations of one specification took byte-identical input, rejected it unanimously, and disagreed about why. Three tested the parse type, so 1e2 fails as a non-integer token. Two tested what the literal denotes, so the integer 100 fails only over how it was spelled. All five reject, which means no accept-or-reject conformance test can observe the split. I wrote all five, so counting them as five independent checks would be counting one opinion five times. Those bytes, and the rest of the corpus they came from, are public at github.com/astrogilda/aee-conformance, so you can run them against your own parser.  In thirty minutes: the live bypass, where the mapping sits relative to the check, the five other recurrences with a runnable artifact for each, and a closing two minutes on a CodeQL query and a Semgrep rule I filed upstream, neither merged, for a defect class the default packs carry no rule for. You leave able to point at the exact line in your own stack where the bytes you checked stop being the bytes that get used.
